title: How to create Claude skills: What your team actually needs
content:
Claude skills help teams save repeatable workflows as instructions that apply automatically — without pasting a long prompt into every chat. A team writes the workflow once, and Claude applies the skill every time.
Creating a Claude skill doesn’t require coding or deep technical knowledge for most business workflows. A skill only needs instructions in plain English. Then, the built-in Claude skill creator can generate a file through a guided conversation.
The article explains what Claude skills can do, how to create a skill, and examples. HubSpot connector for Claude ensures everything a team makes is informed by real customer data in a CRM.
A Claude skill is a self-contained folder that teaches Claude how to perform a specific task and loads automatically when a matching task comes up. Each skill folder contains a required SKILL.md file and may also include references, assets, or scripts. The skill loads only when the task matches the skill capability. Claude skills are available on all plans.
Skills can be made by chatting with Claude in plain language — no coding required. Users just describe the workflow and save it as a new Claude skill. Marketers and RevOps professionals can use a Claude skill creator without a technical background.
Users just describe the workflow and save it as a new Claude skill. For example, a content marketer may use their brand guidelines to build an editing skill. Or, a learning and development expert may build a skill to help write SOPs.
Teams need a developer when a skill bundles Python, Bash, or Node.js scripts, which require debugging. Similarly, if Claude cannot access a system or call a proprietary API, developers need to configure, host, and wire up the connection with authentication and permissions.
Claude skills rely on a progressive disclosure mechanism. Instead of stuffing skill details into the context window up front, Claude loads a skill’s contents in layers, only as much as the task requires. There are three levels at which Claude skills work:
The only text Claude sees when deciding whether to load a particular skill is the skill description. A vague or overlapping skill description causes trigger confusion. Since the description is the trigger, write it to match intent, and the rest of the skill only ever loads when it should.
For example, Claude’s official documentation offers this example: “Apply Acme Corp brand guidelines to presentations and documents, including official colors, fonts, and logo usage.”
Marketers who don’t know how to code can use the skill creator in Claude. Start by scoping the task. Then, clarify the skill’s inputs and outputs, as well as any specifications on how to handle sensitive data.
Skill creation begins with a focused, repeatable workflow and a defined success condition. Pick one workflow, such as writing release notes or generating a weekly report. Multiple small skills compose better than one large one, so keep each skill focused on a single job.
Write down the trigger (what the user says), the inputs (what users provide), and the output (what users get back). If users can’t state all three in a sentence, the scope is too broad.
The body of a SKILL.md file must spell out exactly what Claude should expect to receive. For non-coders, inputs can typically be a pasted text block — that may include a meeting transcript or raw notes. Users can also upload files, like a .docx or image.
Be explicit in the inputs to remove ambiguity and stop Claude from guessing. Users can even program Claude to ask specific questions before starting.
Describe the exact shape of what Claude should produce, such as format, structure, tone, and length. A common way to do this is to put a template file in an assets/ subfolder and reference it from SKILL .md . If the instructions map a format to that template, Claude will use it for the output file when the user asks for that format.
Users should not hardcode secret or personal data in a SKILL.md file or in bundled reference files. Don’t include classified customer data, internal schemas, or confidential documents as examples. Always use anonymized or representative, hypothetical samples.
Make sure any API that a skill calls is compliant with company policies or industry regulations. State in SKILL.md what data the skill expects, what it produces, and where it sends anything. A security or compliance reviewer can easily assess the skill without reading every line of logic.
There are major differences between writing concise instructions in plain English and writing executable code. What a team wants to build determines whether a developer should get involved or if non-technical professionals can get the job done.
Prose instructions are better for language-heavy workflows like writing and summarizing. Non-technical professionals can write skills that follow specific step-by-step instructions that must be handled the same way every time — all without coding. Claude will generate the script for a specific skill, but users may need to review it for inaccuracies, which may be difficult without technical knowledge.
Marketers can create a skill from scratch using the built-in Claude skill creator. To do so, users need to name the skill, describe it, and explain what the skill should do through specific instructions. From there, marketers can add additional materials as references.
Below is a step-by-step process that outlines the complete guide to building skills for Claude. To demonstrate, I’ve built a skill designed to prepare a marketing campaign performance report.
Make a folder named after the skill. The front matter sits between two “---” lines at the top of SKILL.md and contains two mandatory fields, “name’ and ‘description.”
Here’s an example pulled from Anthropic’s pre-installed marketing skills:
description: Build a marketing performance report with key metrics, trend analysis, wins and misses, and prioritized optimization recommendations…
Everything below the closing “---” after the front matter is the body of Claude skills. The Markdown instructions are the actual prompt Claude follows when the skill fires. Write it in numbered steps, in the third person, with explicit inputs and outputs. Keep the instructions tight, so it’s easier for Claude to follow.
- **Campaign report** — performance of a specific campaign
- **Channel report** — performance across a specific channel (email, social, paid, SEO, etc.)
- **Content performance** — how content pieces are performing
- **Overall marketing report** — cross-channel summary (weekly, monthly, quarterly)
Claude follows a progressive disclosure method. Instructions in SKILL.md tell Claude when to open each reference file. Use the references for material that’s too long to put inline but is necessary for specific branches of the task.
For example, reference files are stored in the following way:
A line in the SKILL.md file, such as the following, can trigger the references:
Before writing the executive summary, read `references/brand-voice.md` and match its tone. If a channel’s ROAS is below the benchmark in ‘references/channel-benchmarks.md’, note the gap explicitly.
Assets are raw materials for the output. Claude doesn’t read them to decide what to do. It copies them, fills them in, or builds on top of them. For example, assets for a marketing campaign performance report can look like the following:
Then, a line in the SKILL.md file can trigger the assets:
Use the structure in `assets/brief-template.md` as the skeleton for the output. Fill in the placeholders. Do not add or remove sections.
Scripts are for deterministic, or pre-determined, step-based operations that must produce the same result every time. That may include parsing, computation, validation, and file transforms. For example, scripts for a campaign performance report look like the following:
Users don’t need technical knowledge to create Claude skills. However, for cross-application workflows, it’s best practice to have a developer review the code before deployment.
The skill description is the only text Claude reads when deciding whether to load a skill. Essentially, the description is a routing rule that Claude evaluates on every turn against a user request. So, users must not confuse the description with a summary or a tagline.
The formula that helps with reliable triggering is:
Here are some rules to write descriptions that trigger reliably.
An inconsistent point of view creates discovery problems when Claude is scanning 100+ skills. Write as if describing the skill to a new colleague, such as, “Use when the user asks…” .
Front-loading the trigger makes the match clearer, so lead with the firing condition.
The second version works easily because the trigger lands in the first five words. The first version buries it at the end, where Claude may not weigh it as heavily.
A single trigger phrase is too narrow because users say the same thing in different ways. The description should name the family of phrasings rather than just one canonical version.
A practical method is to write down every way a user or the team would naturally phrase the request in the last month. Then pick the five to seven highest-signal variants. List them to give Claude the semantic range it needs to match a loosely worded request to the right skill.
For example: “ Use when the user says “release notes, “ “ changelog, “ “ what shipped, “ “ summarize this diff, “ “ write the release summary,” or pastes a git diff and asks for a formatted output.”
One of the key issues of broad coverage is over-triggering. A skill can activate on adjacent requests it was never designed for. Therefore, teams should have strict “do NOT” clauses, especially when there are multiple skills in the same domain.
For example, a “release notes” skill and a “changelog” skill will collide without explicit exclusions. So, mention explicitly: “Do NOT use for general git operations (commit, push, rebase), for PR review, or for summarizing documentation changes.”
Claude has a tendency to undertrigger skills to handle a task with its base capabilities rather than loading a skill that would do it better. To counteract undertriggering, use slightly assertive language in the “use when” clause, such as:
Although the max limit is 1,024 characters, long descriptions can dilute the message. Claude scans dozens of descriptions, and a wall of text is harder to match against than a tight, specific one. If a description is over 400 characters, users are probably restating the body or listing too many trigger variants. Cut to the highest-signal phrases and move the rest into the SKILL.md body.
Write the body first, get the workflow, inputs, and outputs right. Then, distill the description from the finished skill. When a user writes the description last, it prevents a common mistake where the description promises something the body doesn’t actually do. Summarizing a finished procedure accurately is much easier than guessing at trigger phrasing.
Run each query three times. Claude’s trigger decision is probabilistic, so a single run can give a false positive or false negative. Three runs per query gives a reliable rate (0/3, 1/3, 2/3, 3/3).
If the should-trigger rate is below 80%, the description is too narrow, or the trigger phrases don’t match real language. Add variants, make the language slightly pushier, or front-load the condition. If the should-not-trigger rate is above 20%, the description is too broad. Tighten the scope and add a “do NOT use” clause.
Every time a user catches a false positive, update the description and re-run the affected eval queries.
Claude skills use cases differ widely by team. While a marketing team might use Claude to generate brand copy, sales departments typically focus more on lead management. Here are common use cases across marketing, sales, and service departments.
In marketing, the same briefs and checklists can apply across channels. The right skill creates brand consistency and lets marketers focus on improving campaigns and content.
Brief writing is a common task in marketing, and marketers are most likely to skip a section in a hurry. The campaign brief skill takes a product launch note, target audience, and channel list as input. Then, it outputs a structured brief with objectives, KPIs, audience segments, messaging angles, and a channel-by-channel execution plan.
Pro tip: I usually add a research element to my campaign brief generator skill. An X add-on helps Claude research breaking news on a topic, understand a founder’s voice, and benchmark my content across other competitors. All of the above research helps Claude generate better and tailored briefs for my clients.
In the content QA and brand voice skill, AI assistants scan or generate a draft for a piece of content against bundled references or a brand voice markdown file. The skill follows a checklist of rules that factors for tone, banned phrases, CTA format, link hygiene, and accessibility. The skill then returns a pass/fail report with specific line-level flags.
Instead of depending on a reviewer to catch brand-voice drift, a QA skill helps the author get a second opinion in minutes. Reference files also guide Claude when it writes new copy, so drafts start closer to the brand standard.
Aaron Beashel, marketer at Converly.io , swears by an open-source GitHub library of pre-made Claude skills built by Corey Haines.
He says, “If I ask Claude to come up with five headlines for an ad, or five social media posts for a blog post, Claude would call up and use those skills to shape its response. The responses are much better because the skills teach Claude what a good social media post, Google Ads headline, or email subject line actually looks like.”
The UTM governance and link audit skill starts with a list of active campaign URLs (from a sheet, a HubSpot view, or pasted text). It then flags missing, malformed, or inconsistent UTM parameters against the naming convention. The skill then outputs a correction table ready to paste back into the tracker.
Once a link loses its parameters, attribution is gone forever, and the audit is tedious. A check done via a UTM governance skill makes sure customers are landing on the right link.
Sales skills help teams personalize leads, follow-ups, and sales calls at scale. Skills can help generate the structure for strong outreach. All the rep needs to do is personalize and review.
A lead triage and routing skill takes a new inbound lead and scores it against the ICP criteria, routing rules, and capacity constraints. The skill then recommends an owner, priority tier, and a reason.
Pro tip: Use the HubSpot connector for Claude to allow the skill to work from actual HubSpot contact and company records.
A discovery call skill bundles a question framework, qualification criteria, and a one-page brief template into a single SKILL.md file. Before the call, users can trigger the skill with a prompt like “prep me for the [company name] call,” and Claude researches the company. The skill can surface likely pain points based on industry and size. It can also format tailored discovery questions, a personalized opener, and top objections to prepare for.
Skills can be tailored to help in post-call follow-ups. Federico Donatone, founder of Growth Cab , built a “recap-call” skill for sales follow-up. The skill pulls the real transcript of a call, writes the follow-up email in his tone of voice, attaches the sales deck only when the recipient is external, and saves the email as a draft.
Service skills help support teams handle tickets the same way every time. Unlike AI agents that handle conversations on their own, a skill guides Claude through a defined process while a support rep stays in charge of the response.
A ticket routing skill helps tickets reach the right team faster, reducing total time to respond. A ticket routing skill reads the incoming ticket’s subject, body, and customer tier. Claude can then walk through a decision tree and choose the correct routing path with a suggested first-response template.
Usually, the handoff from service to sales is where expansion opportunities suffer. Context may get lost between teams. When a support ticket mentions a feature request, a pricing question, or an expansion signal, the skill pulls the customer’s account record , recent usage, and open deals, then outputs a one-page brief.
In cases like these, HubSpot CRM serves as the system of record for contacts, deals, interactions, and related business context. Using the HubSpot Connector, the skill can pull customer records from the CRM and present them.
Governance keeps Claude skills accurate and secure after they are deployed. Skills can only do what their permissions allow, so someone needs to own those permissions. Make sure permissions are set properly and that governance best practices are followed.
Since users write skill logic in natural language, the same file can behave differently across model versions. And, a subtle wording change can shift behavior. If someone tampers with a skill, it can affect anything the skill has access to.
Admins in enterprise organizations have some level of control with skill scanning. These admins can check uploaded skills for malicious content, and owners control provisioning.
Every skill in an internal registry should have a named owner responsible for maintenance, security review, and decommissioning. Without an owner, a skill can accumulate out-of-date instructions or get updated by someone who doesn’t understand the security implications.
For a larger org, a designated security team or platform reviewers should sign off before a skill is promoted to the org-wide directory.
Project skills that live in a user’s repository can be opened up to teammates through commits and pull requests. However, an individual user’s skills should be private to that user only.
Users must scrutinize public skills from GitHub, marketplaces, or shared Slack channels before deployment. Read every file in the skill directory, including Markdown instructions, scripts, and assets. Specifically, check for any instructions that would make Claude ignore safety rules or hide actions from users.
Before deploying a skill to an organization, verify script behavior by running bundled scripts in a sandbox. Then, confirm that outputs match the skill’s stated purpose. Any URL, API endpoint, fetch, curl, or requests call is a way for data to leave the company, so audit them carefully.
Claude skills require periodic reviews. Old skills can be a potential risk surface caused by stale instructions, outdated permissions, and abandoned scripts. The following table shows how to set a review cadence for different types of skills.
A marketer or RevOps professional doesn’t need to write all the Claude skills they use. A wide range of pre-built skills, from Anthropic’s own repository to community marketplaces, are already available to choose from.
Teams can choose to build skills, install skills, or take a hybrid. Most teams end up with a mix of approaches, depending on which model best suits their workflows.
Build a skill from scratch when the knowledge is unique to the user, and the repetition is high enough to justify the authoring cost. The main signals to build Claude skills are:
Domain experts such as RevOps analysts, content strategists, or compliance officers can build skills, often with help from an engineer or the Claude Skill Creator to handle the technical packaging. Although technical knowledge isn’t needed, the person must know the workflow well enough to write it down.
Install a pre-built skill when the capability is general, easily solvable, and the source meets the team’s security standards. The main signals to install Claude skills are:
Always make sure skills are run through the security measures discussed earlier in the article.
Anyone with a Claude Code or Claude.ai account can install Claude skills. A user can download skills from Anthropic with the click of a button. For the rest, the technical barrier is a single command (/plugin install <name>@<marketplace>) or a ZIP upload in Claude.ai settings.
A hybrid model installs a generic skill that handles the mechanics, then builds a thin custom skill that layers the business logic on top. When the installed skill gets an update, the team’s custom rules keep working. When the team’s rules change, they edit only their own files and leave the installed skill alone.

The HubSpot connector for Claude gives skills access to authorized HubSpot CRM data. Claude skills can thus act on real contacts, deals, and tickets from HubSpot instead of pasted text.
The HubSpot connector is the first CRM connector for Claude. Users can ask questions in plain language and generate visualizations like charts and graphs. Moreover, the Connector respects each user’s existing HubSpot permissions, so each rep sees only the records their access allows. The connector is available to all HubSpot customers across all tiers with a paid Claude subscription.
Teams that want to make their skills more powerful with live CRM data can get started with the HubSpot connector for Claude today.
Most Claude skills don’t require coding. If the workflow is judgment-based, natural text instructions are enough. Executable scripts in a scripts/ subfolder are optional and only worth adding for operations like parsing, computation, or validation. Even then, users can describe the expected input and output in plain English instructions and ask Claude to generate the script.
In Claude, custom skills are uploaded to individual user accounts and in Claude Code. The skills live in a local or project .claude/skills folder. On Team and Enterprise plans, organization owners can provision skills for all users, and those skills appear automatically in every team member’s skills list.
Claude loads each skill’s contents in three layers, only as deep as the task requires. At session start, Claude reads just the name and description from every installed skill’s YAML front matter, which is enough to know a skill exists and when it might apply.
When a user request matches a skill’s description, Claude reads the full SKILL.md file body into context and follows its step-by-step instructions. If the instructions reference bundled files, such as reference docs, templates, or scripts, Claude opens only those specific files at the moment it needs them.
Users often confuse the Claude skills vs. commands distinction. A Claude skill is a folder built around a SKILL.md file. The skill teaches Claude how to perform one task. A slash command is a short, user-invoked prompt shortcut (/commit, /review). Whereas a plugin is a distribution package that bundles multiple skills, slash commands, hooks, subagents, and MCP server configurations into a single installable unit.
Teams can share and govern Claude skills across an organization. Anthropic supports centrally deployable skills through managed settings or a shared repository that syncs to every developer’s machine.
Creating a good skill depends more on process knowledge than technical skill. Data can also help improve outputs. The HubSpot connector for Claude provides additional customer context and business information by giving skills access to authorized HubSpot data.
My advice? Take advantage of the pre-built Claude skills made by Anthropic and experienced marketers across industries. I often try to reverse engineer how they work by using them extensively and reading their SKILL.md file. That habit has made my own custom skills much better.
Start with one workflow, pair it with a well-written SKILL.md and live HubSpot data, and measure the time it saves. Once the first one works, building the next skill gets a lot easier.
